explanation: This opening establishes the course as an implementation-oriented study of database systems. The professor also stresses that exercises are the interactive part of the course: use the recordings to learn the concepts, but use the exercises to test whether you can apply them and expose gaps in your understanding.

A DBMS is used when data is large, valuable, or both. Its implementation must simultaneously scale to very large datasets, preserve data through software and hardware failures, and support many concurrent users without producing incorrect results. These goals interact: concurrency complicates correctness, recovery complicates storage, and scalability rules out many straightforward algorithms.

The exam-relevant point is why DBMS software is complex. The complexity is not accidental; it is the engineering cost of offering reliable, concurrent, high-performance data management behind a stable interface.

The course has three linked goals: understand the classical architecture used by established DBMSs, learn algorithms for processing large datasets efficiently, and see how hardware trends force architectural changes. Implementation knowledge is useful even when you do not build a DBMS, because it helps you configure and diagnose existing systems.

Keep the course structure as a mental map: storage, access paths, transactions and recovery form the classical foundation; query processing explains how sets of tuples are executed efficiently; the final part revisits those choices for large memories, many-core CPUs, and cache-sensitive execution.

The slides and exercises contain the required course material. The listed textbooks are optional depth: Härder and Rahm is the professor’s preferred treatment of implementation, Garcia-Molina, Ullman, and Widom covers a broader subset, and Gray and Reuter specializes in transaction processing. These books mainly explain classical architectures; modern hardware-oriented material is more often found in research papers.

The motivating task—finding values common to two lists—looks trivial at application scale but exposes the central DBMS problem: scalability. A nested loop is easy to write, yet its cost grows with the product of the input sizes. When relations contain millions of records or no longer fit in memory, the choice of algorithm and data organization dominates the implementation.

Treat this example as a model for the course: begin with a simple logical operation, then ask which physical algorithm remains correct and efficient across large inputs, limited memory, skew, duplicates, and storage failures.

When both lists fit in memory, two strong strategies are available. Sorting both inputs and merging them costs roughly O(n log n), because the final merge scan is linear but sorting dominates. Building a hash table on one input and probing it with the other is expected O(n), assuming a suitable hash function and controlled collisions.

The tempting nested-loop comparison is O(|L1|·|L2|), which becomes infeasible at database scale. The practical rule is to seek O(n log n) or better unless the requested output itself is quadratic. Data structure choice therefore converts the same logical result into radically different runtimes.

If only the smaller list fits in memory, build an in-memory hash table for that list and scan the larger list in chunks. Each chunk is probed against the persistent hash table and can then be discarded. The large input never has to reside in memory as a whole.

This is an important boundary case: one memory-resident build side preserves an essentially linear algorithm. The difficulty rises sharply only when neither input can provide such an in-memory search structure.

If neither input fits in memory, the algorithm must become an external-memory algorithm. One option is external sorting followed by a streaming merge. Another is to partition both inputs with the same rule until corresponding partitions fit in memory, then solve each smaller intersection locally.

The partitioning approach turns one impossible in-memory problem into many manageable ones, but it adds I/O, partition management, and failure cases such as oversized or skewed partitions. The key exam distinction is that external algorithms optimize block transfers and sequential access, not merely CPU comparisons.

A robust DBMS cannot assume clean, uniformly distributed inputs. Duplicates may carry different payloads and must be preserved, and a single extremely frequent key may be too large for an in-memory partition. That breaks the simple claim that repeated partitioning will always make every bucket fit.

A production implementation must detect such skew and handle it specially—for example, separating the heavy key and reconstructing its matches later. The lesson is that scalable database algorithms require infrastructure for corner cases; the apparent four-line problem can become hundreds or thousands of lines when it must work for arbitrary user data.

Large datasets make asymptotic complexity important even when everything fits in memory. Millions or billions of items make quadratic work unacceptable; external storage makes the same problem harder because data movement is far slower than computation.

A DBMS therefore needs a careful software architecture with reusable components for partitioning, sorting, hashing, buffering, and exceptional cases. The objective is not to hand-code a complex scalable algorithm for every query, but to build reliable primitives from which many queries can be assembled.

Loop-oriented code naturally compares one item with another, but nested iteration often creates quadratic work. Set-oriented processing instead hands whole relations or sizeable batches to an operator. That larger unit lets the system sort, hash, partition, or build an index once and reuse the preparation across many tuples.

The distinction is conceptual as well as syntactic: SQL describes a result over sets, while the DBMS chooses a physical set algorithm. Exam questions may ask why set-oriented execution enables better asymptotic complexity than per-record application loops.

Relational algebra supplies the set-oriented primitives used to represent queries. Union, intersection, and difference combine compatible schemas; rename changes attribute identity; projection retains selected attributes; selection filters tuples; product forms every pair; and a join returns only pairs satisfying a predicate. A product may require quadratic output, whereas common joins can often be implemented near the cost of reading both inputs plus producing the result.

The definitions use sets, but SQL normally uses bag semantics, so duplicates are retained unless explicitly removed. That difference matters when deriving equivalent expressions and estimating result sizes.

These derived operators are best learned by their semantics. A natural join equates all same-named attributes and emits one copy of each common attribute; it is convenient in textbooks but less useful internally because compilers normally assign unique column identities. Division expresses an “all” condition: return left-side values related to every value on the right.

A semi-join returns each left tuple that has at least one matching right tuple, corresponding roughly to EXISTS; an anti-join returns left tuples with no match, corresponding roughly to NOT EXISTS. A left outer join adds unmatched left tuples padded with NULLs, while a full outer join also preserves unmatched right tuples. Bag semantics and NULLs require extra care.

The professor switches from the familiar derived operators to extensions needed for real SQL. No substantive explanation occurs in this two-second interval; the map, aggregation, and dependent-join operators are explained in the following interval.

This brief return to the derived-operator slide closes the review of introductory relational algebra. The important definitions are explained on the earlier derived-operators interval; the lecture now moves to operators needed to model full SQL.

Real SQL needs operators beyond the basic algebra. A map computes a new attribute, such as `z = x + y`. Grouping partitions tuples by key attributes and applies aggregate functions. A dependent join evaluates its right-hand expression using values supplied by the current left tuple, which models correlated subqueries.

Naively evaluating the right side once per left tuple is quadratic, so optimizers try to decorrelate dependent joins into ordinary joins by moving the correlation predicate upward. When decorrelation is impossible, the system retains a dependent operator—called `CROSS APPLY` in some systems—and must pay or mitigate its repeated-evaluation cost.

Batching many tuples gives the DBMS room to reorganize data before doing the main operation. It can build indexes, sort, hash, or partition an entire input, turning repeated pairwise work into reusable preparation and efficient scans.

The target is usually O(n log n) or better, except when the user explicitly requests a result whose size is already quadratic. This output-sensitive qualification matters: no algorithm can run faster than the amount of result data it must emit.

Classical DBMS architecture assumed that datasets greatly exceeded main memory, I/O dominated CPU work, and random disk access was exceptionally expensive. A mechanical seek of several milliseconds permits only a few hundred random accesses per second, so designs strongly favor sequential I/O and conservative buffering.

Those assumptions produced scalable systems because they minimized dependence on fast memory and tolerated very large databases. They also shaped page-oriented storage and access algorithms that remain visible in modern products.

Large main memories and SSDs weaken the traditional assumption that disk I/O dominates every query. More data stays resident, random storage access is less catastrophic, and CPU execution and cache behavior become comparatively important. A classical design still works, but it may leave substantial modern-hardware performance unused.

The change is evolutionary rather than a complete reset. Large datasets still require scalable storage algorithms, and even SSDs favor larger, more sequential transfers. Modern DBMS design therefore retains proven techniques while reconsidering cost balances and CPU-oriented execution.

An ideal DBMS handles very large datasets, preserves committed data through failures, exposes a high-level declarative interface, hides physical data-management complexity, and delivers strong performance across varied queries and distributions. Skew and duplicates should not make correctness disappear or performance collapse.

Meeting all of these goals in one reusable system demands significant internal complexity. That investment is worthwhile because many applications can share the same carefully engineered DBMS instead of each reimplementing storage, concurrency, and recovery.

The lecture proceeds from physical foundations to execution and then hardware-aware redesign. The classical part covers storage, access paths, transactions, and recovery. Efficient query processing then studies set-at-a-time data flow, physical implementations of algebraic operators, and translation of a query into executable code. The final part revisits storage, cache locality, and transaction processing for modern main-memory and many-core machines.

Use this sequence as a dependency graph: query execution depends on records and indexes; correctness depends on transactions and recovery; modern optimizations modify these layers but do not remove the need to understand them.

This title interval opens the storage unit. The central question is how a DBMS maps application-level records and relations onto persistent physical media while retaining performance, reliability, and independence from the hardware.

Application data sits several abstractions above physical storage: a physical drive may be combined into a logical volume, exposed through a file system, and then translated by DBMS storage components. The DBMS must decide how much of this stack to control itself.

Raw-device access historically offered precise placement and I/O control, but made administration and backup difficult. Modern systems usually use file systems, accepting some loss of low-level control in exchange for portability and operability. Storage architecture is therefore a boundary-design problem, not just a serialization problem.

Storage must provide data independence: applications address logical data, while the DBMS remains free to reorganize files, replace devices, or introduce RAID and network storage. Scalability requires efficient random access and updates even when the dataset is far larger than memory; a selective key lookup must not scan the entire database.

Reliability adds the strongest constraint: once data is committed, software failure, power loss, or device failure must not silently remove or corrupt it. These requirements rule out many simple layouts—for example, one tightly compressed monolithic block may save space but makes individual updates and lookups impractical.

Implementing every storage concern directly wherever it is needed would create an unmaintainable monolith. A layered architecture assigns a specific responsibility and interface to each level, and normally permits communication only between neighboring levels.

This limits the effect of change. Replacing hard disks with SSD-aware storage may require changes in the hardware-facing layer and its immediate consumer, but query processing should remain independent. The same principle appears in network stacks: stable boundaries allow lower-level technology to evolve without rewriting the entire system.

A simplified DBMS stack can be understood by the unit each layer manipulates. The storage layer moves and buffers fixed-size pages. The access layer arranges physical bytes into records and access paths such as indexes. The query layer translates and optimizes declarative queries and consumes or produces sets of logical records.

Each upward interface hides a lower-level decision. Query processing need not know which disk block holds a record, and applications need not know how pages are buffered. This separation makes major physical changes possible without changing the declarative application interface.

Layers progress from physical blocks to pages, records, and finally relations and queries. A lower layer offers a manageable abstraction to the layer above it, keeping each component understandable and replaceable. This three-layer sketch is useful, but a real DBMS needs finer distinctions between physical records, logical records, schemas, buffering, and device access.

The detailed architecture maps each interface to a granularity. A file interface maps logical block requests to storage. The buffer manager maps database page identifiers to resident memory frames. Record access places physical byte records on pages and uses free-space structures. The record interface maps logical keys or record identifiers through access paths such as B-trees. Finally, the query interface translates SQL over relations and views using schemas and integrity constraints.

The value of the diagram is the chain of responsibility: SQL does not directly manipulate blocks. Each step introduces the metadata needed for the next abstraction, so a logical student record can eventually be located as bytes on a physical page.

The layered picture omits two cross-cutting concerns. Transaction isolation prevents concurrent users from observing or producing inconsistent states, while recovery restores a correct durable state after failures. They cannot be confined neatly to one box because storage, buffering, and higher execution layers must coordinate with them.

Implementations also vary at their boundaries: most delegate raw-device access to the operating system, some delegate buffering as well, and a few expose direct logical-record access. These are variations on the architecture rather than a rejection of layering.

The professor points to the bottom of the architecture: modern DBMSs commonly omit their own raw-drive layer and let the operating system map files and blocks to the device. The conceptual interface remains, but responsibility moves below the DBMS.

This short interval introduces a more aggressive delegation choice: some systems also ask the operating system to manage which file pages reside in memory. The following intervals explain why that approach is convenient for reads but difficult for controlled, recoverable writes.

Memory mapping can replace an explicit DBMS buffer interface by mapping a file into the process address space. Reads then look like ordinary memory accesses and the operating system loads pages on demand. The convenience is real, but it also transfers page-eviction and write-timing decisions to the operating system.

Operating-system buffering becomes tricky when pages are modified. With a memory-mapped file, the OS may write any dirty page at any time. If two related pages must reach storage in a controlled order, an unexpected eviction followed by a power failure can leave only half of the logical update persistent.

A DBMS can force writes but cannot generally prevent the OS from writing first, which complicates write-ahead logging and recovery guarantees. This is why direct OS buffering is attractive for read-heavy workloads yet many traditional systems retain their own buffer manager for precise write control.

At the opposite, application-facing end of the stack, a few systems allow clients to bypass SQL and access logical records directly by key or record identifier. This can reduce query-layer overhead, but it exposes a lower-level API and is uncommon in general-purpose relational systems.

This closes the architecture discussion: products may move individual boundaries, but most still follow the same progression from storage blocks to buffered pages, physical and logical records, and declarative queries.

Storage design must follow hardware behavior. Historically, transistor counts, memory capacity, CPU speed, and disk capacity grew rapidly, but these trends diverged: single-core CPU speed stalled because of power and heat, core counts grew instead, and disk capacity increased without comparable improvement in mechanical seek time.

The mismatch matters more than raw capacity. A larger disk whose random access still costs milliseconds makes scattered reads increasingly unattractive. SSDs reduce that latency but introduce different constraints, so a DBMS must optimize for the actual hierarchy rather than assume every hardware metric improves together.

The memory hierarchy trades capacity for latency. CPU registers hold only a tiny number of bytes but are accessible at instruction speed; caches grow from kilobytes to megabytes while becoming slower; main memory provides gigabytes or terabytes at roughly two orders of magnitude higher latency than registers; external storage is larger again but operates in microseconds or milliseconds. Offline media can hold enormous archives but may take seconds or minutes to reach.

A DBMS gains performance by keeping frequently used data as high in this hierarchy as possible. The hierarchy—not merely disk size—explains buffering, cache-conscious layouts, read-ahead, and locality-sensitive algorithms.

Every descent in the memory hierarchy introduces a large latency gap. Traditional systems focused on the main-memory-to-disk gap, but modern high-performance execution must also respect cache-to-memory costs. Maximizing locality means arranging access so recently or frequently needed data remains in the fastest available level.

Mechanical disks have a fundamental asymmetry: sequential throughput can be increased by striping across more drives, but each random request still waits for head movement and rotation. Transfer bandwidth is therefore purchasable; seek latency largely is not. DBMSs respond by arranging data contiguously and favoring scans over scattered page requests.

SSDs reduce random-read latency but still prefer larger transfers and have write-specific issues such as erase-block granularity and finite endurance. The device changes the magnitude of the cost, not the need to understand access patterns.

Pages amortize storage latency by moving a block of data per I/O rather than one tuple at a time. A larger page reduces the number of device operations and improves sequential bandwidth, but may fetch many irrelevant bytes and consume buffer space when a query needs only one record.

That trade-off makes workload important. Transaction processing with selective random access often prefers moderate pages, while analytical scans that consume most bytes can benefit from much larger pages. Traditional 4 KiB pages are therefore not a universal optimum; 16–64 KiB or even larger units may be appropriate.

The page becomes a pervasive DBMS unit: I/O, buffer allocation, and often recovery all operate at page granularity. Yet a page is still too small to eliminate storage latency, so systems try to turn page requests into sequential streams.

Read-ahead detects or knows that a scan is progressing through adjacent pages and fetches upcoming pages asynchronously. Write-back can similarly collect dirty pages, reorder them by location, and write them in larger sequential runs. Both techniques overlap device latency with useful work while preserving the page abstraction.

The buffer manager caches active disk pages in memory. `FIX(page, mode)` pins a page so it cannot be evicted while the caller uses it and requests shared access for reading or exclusive access for possible modification. `UNFIX(page, dirty)` releases the pin and reports whether the contents actually changed.

The distinction between permission and modification matters: an update query may request exclusive access but find no qualifying tuple, leaving the page clean. Dirty pages eventually require persistent write-back and coordination with recovery; clean pages can be discarded immediately when space is needed.

A buffer pool is commonly indexed by a hash table from page number to buffer frame. A frame stores metadata and points to the actual page-sized memory region. Hash collisions form a short chain or another bucket structure, so locating a resident page is expected constant time.

Concurrency makes this structure performance-critical. Every query visits the buffer manager, so one global latch would serialize unrelated page lookups. Implementations partition or latch buckets independently and protect individual frames, allowing threads that access different pages to proceed concurrently.

A buffer frame records the page identifier, a shared/exclusive latch, the page’s latest log sequence number, state such as clean, dirty, or newly created, and a pointer to the page data. The LSN supports write-ahead logging: before a dirty page reaches disk, the log describing its changes must be durable.

Latch design must avoid blocking unrelated pages in the same hash bucket. A thread waiting for page P1 must not retain a bucket latch that prevents another thread from reaching P2. Frame metadata also carries replacement information so the manager can choose an eviction victim.

When the pool is full, a clean victim can be discarded, whereas a dirty victim must first be written. The theoretical optimum evicts the page whose next use lies farthest in the future, but future requests are unknown; random eviction is implementable but ignores all workload information.

Practical policies approximate the optimum using recent behavior at modest bookkeeping cost. The exam trade-off is not only hit rate: a policy that predicts slightly better can still lose if synchronization and metadata maintenance make every page access expensive.

FIFO keeps frames in arrival order and evicts the oldest. It is cheap—a linked queue needs only insertion at the tail and removal from the head—but it does not recognize hot pages. A page repeatedly accessed since loading can still be evicted simply because it arrived early.
FIFO can even exhibit Belady’s anomaly, where adding buffer capacity increases the number of misses. Its simplicity makes it a useful baseline, not a strong general DBMS replacement policy.

LRU approximates future usefulness with recency. Frames form a doubly linked list; an unfixed page moves to the tail, and eviction removes the least recently used frame at the head. Repeatedly accessed pages therefore remain near the protected end.

The policy is popular, but exact LRU turns the list into a synchronization hotspot: every access may unlink and relink an entry, and many worker threads compete over shared list state. A theoretically better victim choice can thus be undermined by the cost of maintaining the order.

The lecture switches from recency to frequency. LFU will rank pages by how often they have been accessed rather than when they were last touched; the next interval explains why that plausible policy is usually too costly.
This brief visual return contrasts LRU’s simple ordered list with the priority structure required by LFU. No new policy is developed here; the frequency-based cost is explained immediately afterward.

LFU counts accesses and evicts the page with the smallest count. Although frequency can identify persistently hot data, keeping frames in an up-to-date priority queue is more expensive than maintaining LRU’s list. The bookkeeping and synchronization overhead generally outweigh the improved prediction, so exact LFU is uncommon in production buffer pools.

Second-chance, also called clock, cheaply approximates LRU with one reference bit per frame and a rotating hand. Access sets the bit. During eviction, the hand clears set bits and skips those pages; the first page encountered with an already-clear bit is selected.

A recently reused page receives another revolution before eviction, while an untouched page eventually loses its protection. The policy stores far less ordering information than exact LRU and avoids a constantly updated global list, making it attractive under high concurrency despite its cruder prediction.

2Q distinguishes pages seen once from pages proven to be reused. A new page enters a FIFO queue. If it is referenced again while still present, it is promoted into an LRU-managed hot queue. Eviction preferentially removes from the FIFO side, while retaining genuinely reused pages longer.

This fits DBMS workloads: a large table scan touches many pages once and should not flush a frequently used B-tree root from memory. 2Q learns that distinction from behavior without treating every first access as evidence of long-term value.

The query engine often knows more than a generic replacement policy can infer. It knows whether a page belongs to a sequential scan, which is unlikely to be revisited, or to an index path, which may be accessed repeatedly. It can pass `will-not-need` or `will-need` hints when unfixing the page.

Hints let the buffer manager place frames nearer the eviction or protected end of its queues. This cross-layer communication adds implementation complexity, but usually outperforms blind statistical policies because it uses the planned access pattern directly.
No aligned speech occurs in this brief closing board frame.

A page is the right transfer unit for buffering and I/O, but relations, indexes, and internal inventories normally span many pages. A segment groups such pages into one manageable entity. Higher layers can grow, scan, or drop the entire structure without tracking every physical page themselves.

A segment resembles a file or virtual address space, but it need not preserve physical or insertion order. Pages allocated later may fill holes between older extents. That freedom improves space utilization and locality while matching relational semantics, where row order is undefined unless a query requests `ORDER BY`.

A segment interface allocates and releases pages, iterates through all pages, and can deallocate the whole collection. These operations support common tasks directly: insertion grows a relation, B-tree merging may release a page, a table scan iterates, and `DROP TABLE` frees the segment.

Linearity is optional. Guaranteeing that logical iteration follows allocation order requires either contiguous placement or extra ordering metadata, so ordinary segments omit that guarantee unless a data structure truly needs it.

The board example shows why segment pages need not be contiguous. Relation R1 is allocated, R2 is placed after it, and later R1 grows again. Dropping R2 leaves a hole that a future R1 allocation can reuse instead of extending the database file.

Physical scan order may consequently differ from insertion order. This is legal because a relation is unordered, and it reduces fragmentation by reusing available space rather than leaving permanent gaps.

The slide returns as the professor begins refining allocation. A segment may request new pages without dictating their exact physical location; the allocator can exploit existing holes and may return a differently sized run than the caller initially expected.

A useful allocation API accepts a minimum and a preferred number of pages. The minimum must be satisfied; the preferred size says how much the caller can exploit. The allocator may even return more to consume an awkward hole completely instead of leaving a tiny unusable fragment.

The caller keeps the extra pages for future insertions. This over-allocation improves long-term physical layout and sequential scans, but further demonstrates why segment iteration cannot be assumed to match insertion order. If result order matters, SQL must state it explicitly.

A linear segment guarantees that logical pages are visited in allocation order. It can enforce this through physical append-only placement or by keeping metadata that reconstructs the order even when pages occupy holes elsewhere.

That guarantee costs space or flexibility, so ordinary relation segments usually omit it. The segment abstraction remains valuable because it hides whichever page mapping policy is chosen from higher layers.

Three mappings connect a logical segment to physical pages. Static mapping stores one start and length, making lookup cheap but growth difficult. Dynamic block mapping stores every page separately, maximizing flexibility at the cost of large metadata and an extra indirection.

Dynamic extent mapping is the practical compromise: each catalog entry describes a consecutive run of pages. A segment grows by adding extents, retaining flexible placement while keeping metadata much smaller and preserving useful sequential runs.

Static mapping minimizes overhead but is hard to resize; per-block mapping resizes freely but creates large page tables and more indirection. Extent mapping grows dynamically with only modest metadata. For general DBMS segments, extents normally offer the best balance of flexibility, lookup cost, and sequential layout.

Extent sizes should grow geometrically, for example by a factor near 1.25. Geometric growth bounds the number of extents logarithmically: even a very large segment then needs only hundreds of mapping entries rather than one entry per page.

The bounded catalog can often fit in one page, reducing lookup complexity and metadata I/O. Larger later extents also create long contiguous page runs, which improve sequential scans. The growth factor trades space slack against catalog size; doubling is easy to illustrate but may over-allocate too aggressively.
The diagram returns to emphasize the consequence of geometric extent growth: unlike a per-page map, the extent catalog has a practical upper bound and can remain a compact, predictable structure.

With geometric growth, only a limited number of extent descriptors is needed before the address space itself is exhausted. Keeping that mapping compact simplifies implementation and makes it plausible to store the complete extent list on one page. Consecutive pages within each growing extent also shift I/O toward faster sequential access.

Segments differ along independent dimensions. Public segments represent user-visible objects; private ones store internal metadata. Permanent segments must survive restarts, while temporary segments hold disposable query intermediates. Automatic segments are always accessible; manual segments historically required an operator to mount media. Recovery-enabled segments pay logging and restoration costs, whereas reconstructible or temporary data may avoid them.

The classification changes implementation cost. A temporary sort run can ignore partial writes because it will be discarded after a crash, while a permanent relation cannot. Some systems may even rebuild indexes rather than recover them, trading cheaper normal updates for rare reconstruction time.

A single page write is not automatically atomic. If power fails during a 16 KiB write, only part of the page may have reached storage, leaving a torn page. A battery-backed device can promise to finish buffered writes, but ordinary hardware may not.

Permanent storage must therefore use recovery techniques—potentially writing protected copies or logging—to detect and repair partial writes. Temporary data can accept the risk because its entire segment is discarded after restart.

Knowing a segment’s lifetime changes the safe write path. A temporary segment needs no expensive guarantee that every page survives a crash. A permanent segment must guard against torn writes and may require redundant writing or logging. Segment metadata therefore guides both storage placement and recovery effort.

Two private low-level structures organize the database. The segment inventory maps each segment to its extents or pages. The free-space inventory records which pages are completely free and, often separately, how much room remains inside allocated pages for new records.

Higher-level segments are built on these foundations: catalogs store schemas, relation segments store tuples, temporary segments hold query intermediates, and index segments store access paths. The inventories are analogous to filesystem directories and allocation maps, but tailored to database pages and record placement.

Steal and force answer different questions. Steal permits eviction of a dirty page containing an uncommitted update, so recovery must later undo that update if the transaction aborts. Force writes every page changed by a transaction at commit, simplifying restart but making commits perform many random writes.

Most systems prefer steal/no-force: memory can be reused freely and commit need only make the log durable, not every data page. This quadrant delivers flexibility and throughput but requires both undo for uncommitted changes that reached disk and redo for committed changes whose pages had not.

The lecture turns from steal/no-force recovery to transaction visibility. An uncommitted update must not be exposed to other transactions, and the next intervals consider shadow paging as a way to preserve both an old committed version and a private modified version.

Locking an entire modified page until commit would hide dirty data, but it also blocks unrelated readers and sharply reduces concurrency. The design challenge is to keep a committed version readable while another transaction prepares changes—and still recover if either the transaction or the machine fails.
This brief return states the recovery problem: under steal, an uncommitted page version may already be on disk when the system crashes. Restart must be able to identify and remove that update.

Shadow paging implements updates by copy-on-write. A logical page table initially points to committed physical pages. Modifying a logical page allocates a new physical copy, applies the change there, and leaves the old copy intact. Readers can continue using the committed mapping.

Abort discards the shadow copy; commit atomically installs the new mapping and frees obsolete pages. Because the old state remains available, recovery and isolation are conceptually simple. The cost is an extra lookup through the mapping and increasingly scattered physical placement.

Shadow paging always retains a clean committed copy, so abort and crash recovery can revert by changing metadata rather than replaying many data changes. Separate mappings can also present different page versions to concurrent transactions.

Its drawbacks are on the normal access path: every logical page requires mapping, and copy-on-write moves updated pages away from their neighbors. The second cost is decisive for disk-based systems because it destroys sequential locality.

The original layout forms one sequential run, but copied pages create several disjoint runs. A scan that formerly required one seek can now require a seek for each fragment. Shadow paging therefore converts a metadata-friendly recovery technique into a storage-locality problem.

Mechanical disks make shadow paging unattractive because every fragment may add a seek. SSDs reduce the penalty, and main memory largely removes page-to-page seek cost, so copy-on-write versioning can still be useful for in-memory isolation.

The general lesson is that an algorithm’s value depends on hardware: the same extra indirection and loss of physical contiguity can be unacceptable on disk yet affordable when pages are memory-resident.

A delta-file strategy also preserves two versions, but groups copies separately. Before changing a page, the system stores either its clean original in the delta and updates the main page, or stores the dirty version in the delta while leaving the main page clean.

Putting clean pages in the delta makes commit cheap—discard the delta—but abort requires copying originals back. Putting dirty pages there reverses the trade-off. The choice therefore optimizes the common outcome, normally commit, while retaining enough information for rollback and isolation.

The professor finishes the two delta-file variants: if modified pages live in the delta, abort is essentially free because the clean main file is already valid, while commit must copy the new versions into place.

Because successful transactions are expected to dominate, a common policy stores clean originals in the delta and writes changes in the main file. Commit then only discards the saved originals; abort pays the rarer copy-back cost. Choosing the opposite layout would optimize abort instead.

Delta files preserve the main file’s physical layout after the transaction completes, avoiding the permanent fragmentation created by shadow paging. They also keep clean and changed versions in clearly separated locations, which simplifies reasoning about recovery. Preserved locality is the professor’s main reason to prefer them.

The locality benefit is purchased with extra I/O. Before an in-place update becomes safe, the original page must be copied to durable delta storage. The later modified-page write still occurs, so every first update to a page introduces an additional write.

Delta files add I/O, make either commit or abort expensive depending on which version is stored separately, and require concurrency-safe tracking of copied pages. Nevertheless, they often beat shadow paging for disk-resident data because committed pages return to a compact, sequential main layout.

When comparing the strategies, distinguish recovery simplicity from steady-state scan performance: shadow paging favors easy version switching, while delta files spend more write work to protect locality.
This title interval closes low-level storage and introduces access paths: the data structures used to organize stored records and reach selected items without scanning an entire relation.

The access layer needs distinct structures for four jobs: locate free space for incoming records, represent ordinary relation data, handle values larger than one page, and accelerate selective lookup with indexes. Treating them separately prevents one layout from being forced to satisfy incompatible requirements.
The sequence of the next chapters follows these dependencies: first decide where a record can fit, then how a page stores it, then how overflow data is represented, and finally how an index finds it.

A free-space inventory answers which page can accept an incoming tuple of a given size. Pages may have different remaining capacity, so a small record can fit where a larger one cannot; this is another reason physical row order differs from insertion order.

A traditional inventory stores a tiny fill-status code—often four bits—for every page. Insertion scans for a sufficiently empty page, places the tuple, and updates the code if the page crosses a fill threshold. The compact summary avoids inspecting every data page directly.

Four bits provide only sixteen fill classes, so the inventory necessarily approximates exact free space. A linear scale is simple but wastes precision near a full page: on a 16 KiB page, one class spans roughly 1 KiB, making the final small gaps hard to use.

A logarithmic or hybrid scale represents small remaining capacities more precisely and coarser large capacities adequately. A hand-designed table can reserve fine classes for 8, 16, 32, and 64 bytes and use linear ranges elsewhere. Whether codes represent used or free bytes is equivalent as long as comparisons are consistent.

A naive insert computes the required class and scans the inventory linearly for a matching page. The inventory is compact—one 16 KiB inventory page can describe hundreds of megabytes—but repeated scans still become a bottleneck as segments grow.

Because there are only a few classes, cache the first or next candidate for each class. Most pages become stable and full, while segments usually grow near the end, so the cached frontier moves forward and avoids rescanning old entries. Deletions may invalidate the hint, but are infrequent enough that repair is cheap.

Allocation benefits from knowing that more data is coming. `allocate(min, max)` states the bytes or pages required now and the larger amount the caller can use soon—for example, while materializing many tuples from `INSERT … SELECT` or storing a large object.

The allocator can choose a nearby run closer to `max`, improving locality and reducing future fragmentation. Segment growth may even over-allocate beyond the hint to consume an inconvenient hole. The contract is deliberately richer than a simple request for an exact number of bytes.

The board compares database allocation with a dynamic vector. A vector may ask `malloc` for 88 bytes while the allocator internally reserves a 96-byte size class. Standard interfaces guarantee only the requested size, so the vector cannot portably exploit the extra eight bytes and may reallocate earlier than necessary.

A database allocator exposes usable capacity deliberately through minimum, preferred, or returned-size information. This lets higher layers consume rounded-up space instead of leaving hidden fragments, illustrating how a richer cross-layer contract can improve layout.

Over-allocation is a deliberate anti-fragmentation tool: return more capacity when that consumes an otherwise awkward gap, and let the caller use it for future growth. Database systems routinely expose this information, whereas general-purpose allocation APIs often hide it.

This interval previews the next implementation step. The free-space inventory chooses a page with enough room; a slotted-page layout then has to place the tuple bytes inside that fixed-size page and preserve a stable way to find them. The full explanation begins in the next recording.
This is a one-word closing board interval; it contains no additional database concept.

A slotted page stores tuple bytes in a fixed-size page and addresses each tuple by `(page id, slot id)`. The slot provides indirection: if an update makes a tuple too large for its original page, the tuple can move elsewhere while the original slot stores a forwarding identifier. Indexes can keep the stable original TID instead of updating every reference.

Forwarding is kept to one hop by updating the original slot whenever the overflow tuple moves again. Point access may read a second page, but a table scan ignores forwarding stubs and later encounters the relocated tuple at its physical destination.
The view zooms from tuple identifiers to one page’s internal layout. Slots and tuple data will grow from opposite ends so the number of records can adapt to variable tuple sizes.

Whether slots are drawn at the front or the end is an implementation detail. What matters is the indirection they provide and the fact that slot metadata and record bytes consume the same finite page space.

Slots grow from one side of the page and tuple bytes from the other; the page becomes full when the two regions meet. This avoids reserving a fixed number of slots before knowing whether incoming variable-length records are tiny or large.

Deletes initially leave holes, and shrinking updates do the same. The page records the reclaimable space but postpones compaction until contiguous free space is actually needed, amortizing the cost of moving records. A growing update is handled like delete plus insert and may use forwarding if it no longer fits locally.

The page header tracks an LSN for recovery, the number of slots, a hint to the first reusable slot, the boundary where packed tuple data begins, and total free space after compaction. Total reclaimable space can exceed the currently contiguous gap when deleted records leave holes.

A page may hold hundreds or a thousand small records, so seemingly harmless linear searches can create quadratic insertion time. Caching the first free slot avoids rescanning an ever-growing slot array on every insert; compaction is likewise delayed until needed.

A normal slot stores an offset into the page and the record length. The pair `(0, 0)` can mark an unused slot. A real zero-length tuple must remain distinguishable, so it uses a nonzero offset with length zero.

This small encoding detail preserves semantics: an empty record exists and has a stable TID, while a free slot can be reused. Database page formats need explicit representations for such boundary cases because every bit pattern may otherwise be ambiguous.

Transactions create a difficult undo case. T1 deletes or shrinks item i1, T2 fills the released space with i2 and commits, then T1 aborts and must restore the larger i1. The original page no longer has room—not even necessarily enough for a forwarding record.

A design that stores forwarding metadata in the data area may have to relocate both items and coordinate several pages during undo. The example motivates reserving forwarding capability inside every slot, where recovery can always find fixed space.

A forwarding record itself consumes bytes—typically at least a TID-sized value. Therefore “move the tuple and leave a pointer” is not safe when another committed update has filled every byte of the original page.

One workaround would move both the restored record and the record that consumed its space, leaving two forwarding entries across several pages. That is logically possible but makes locking, recovery, and failure handling unnecessarily complex. The slot representation should prevent this cascade.

Reserve enough slot bits to hold either the ordinary `(offset, length)` pair or a full forwarding TID. A tag or otherwise invalid TID pattern distinguishes the two interpretations. Undo can then redirect a restored record even when the page’s data area is completely full, because the slot space already exists.

The slot may be larger than the minimum offset-and-length encoding, but that small per-record cost removes a difficult multi-page recovery case. This is a classic systems trade-off: spend a predictable few bytes to simplify correctness.

For pages up to 64 KiB, two-byte offset and length fields would fit in four bytes. A forwarding TID may require eight bytes, so the unified slot format can double slot overhead. The professor argues that the simpler recovery and redirection logic is worth this space.

The recommended design uses one eight-byte slot format for both local records and forwarding TIDs. This guarantees that the slot can represent a redirect without allocating additional tuple-data space, eliminating the “page too full to undo” failure mode.

With forwarding stored directly in the fixed slot, an abort can always restore the logical tuple by placing its bytes elsewhere and updating that slot. The committed tuple that filled the page does not need to move, so recovery stays local and predictable.

The professor emphasizes this as an implementation recommendation, not merely notation: encode a moved tuple’s TID inside the slot itself. The exercise implementation is intended to make the resulting simplification in updates and undo concrete.

One eight-byte slot encoding uses a tag to distinguish a forwarding TID from a local record descriptor. In the local case, the remaining fields give offset and length plus a flag saying whether the record was relocated from another page.

A relocated record stores its original TID in the first bytes of its data. That extra identity is needed during scans: the scanner encounters the record at its new physical page but must report the stable original TID used by indexes and later updates.

Index lookup starts from the stable original TID, reaches the forwarding slot, and follows one hop to the moved tuple. A table scan behaves differently: it ignores the forwarding stub on the original page and emits the record only when it reaches the destination page.

At that destination, the scan reports the stored original TID rather than the new physical location. This prevents duplicates during the scan and ensures a subsequent update or delete addresses the same logical tuple that indexes reference.

The “moved” flag and original TID make relocation invisible to a sequential scan. The scan avoids following random pointers, reads the tuple once at its destination, and still emits its stable logical identifier. Relocation therefore penalizes point access but not the sequential scan path.

After a slot locates a tuple byte range, the DBMS still needs an efficient layout inside that record. Naively serializing fields in declaration order works for storage, but variable-length attributes make later fields expensive to locate: the system must read and add every preceding variable length.

With many columns, access becomes O(number of preceding attributes). A DBMS therefore stores metadata that permits direct positioning rather than parsing the record from the beginning for each requested column.

The improved layout separates a fixed-size header from a variable-size tail. Fixed-width values and offsets occupy known header positions; strings and other variable data are packed in the tail. This makes direct attribute access possible.
This two-second interval only labels the example attributes while the professor switches between diagrams. The fixed-header/variable-tail construction continues in the following interval.

The professor maps the example columns to their fixed and variable positions. No new rule is introduced here; the next interval explains why end offsets, rather than lengths, provide constant-time access.

For each variable-length field, store its end offset in the fixed header. The field’s start is the previous field’s end—or the end of the fixed header for the first variable field—and its length is the difference between consecutive end offsets.

This avoids summing all preceding lengths. Fixed-width fields already occupy compile-time offsets, and a variable field needs only two offset reads and a subtraction. Every attribute is therefore reachable in O(1), even in a wide tuple.
Constant-time positioning is not the only layout goal. The lecture now considers hardware alignment and explains why the physical column order should differ from the SQL declaration order.

The current layout still preserves declaration order within the fixed header. The next step deliberately reorders physical fields while retaining a schema mapping so logical SQL column order remains unchanged.

Treat a variable-length string as fixed metadata plus variable data, then order all fixed-width items by decreasing alignment requirement and place the byte-oriented tails last. This setup avoids misaligned fields without inserting padding; the board interval develops the hardware reason.

A value is aligned when its address is a multiple of its required alignment—typically its size for primitive types. An eight-byte integer prefers an address divisible by eight; a four-byte integer prefers one divisible by four. Some processors trap on misaligned access, while others execute it with possible penalties, especially across cache-line boundaries.

If fields remain in arbitrary declaration order, a one-byte value can push the next four-byte integer to a misaligned offset. The physical record layout should therefore arrange fields to satisfy alignment independently of the logical schema.

Sorting primitive fields by decreasing alignment guarantees correct offsets because the alignments are powers of two. Place eight-byte fields first, then four-byte, two-byte, one-byte, and finally variable byte arrays. Each accumulated offset remains divisible by the next requirement.

A language compiler that cannot reorder declared fields inserts padding before a misaligned field, wasting record space. The DBMS owns its private byte format and can reorder safely, so it obtains aligned access without padding. Schema metadata maps logical columns back to their physical positions.

SQL NULL represents a value outside a column’s ordinary domain. If a column is declared `NOT NULL`, the record needs no NULL representation, so that constraint can improve storage and access. A nullable column needs either a reserved sentinel or separate metadata.

Reserving an ordinary value is often impossible because every bit pattern is legal—for example, for integers. A separate NULL bitmap preserves the complete domain. It costs a bit per nullable attribute but can also allow the physical value bytes to be omitted when NULLs are common.

Using the minimum signed integer as a NULL sentinel looks convenient but changes valid arithmetic. Two ordinary values can produce that bit pattern, causing a computed non-NULL result to be mistaken for NULL. Preventing the mistake requires checks after arithmetic and still removes a legitimate value from the SQL domain.

The board’s overflow example demonstrates the general rule: a representation that borrows a valid domain value leaks complexity into every operation. Explicit NULL metadata is usually safer and semantically correct.

A NULL bitmap cleanly separates presence from value: if the bit is set, value bytes are ignored; otherwise the full underlying domain remains available. This avoids sentinel arithmetic and comparison bugs.

A compact format may also omit bytes for NULL fields, saving space when missing values are frequent. That “NULL compression” makes offsets and access logic more complicated, so it is a workload trade-off: use explicit bits for correctness, and omit payload bytes only when the space and bandwidth savings justify variable layout.

DBMS compression is usually a performance optimization, not primarily a way to save money on disk. Halving the bytes read can roughly halve bandwidth-bound I/O time, and smaller records also improve cache and memory utilization.

Compression succeeds only if decompression costs less than the data movement it removes. Embedded systems may care directly about capacity, but server systems normally choose compression schemes by end-to-end query speed rather than the smallest possible representation.

The lecture introduces two design questions: how large a unit to compress, and which algorithm to use. Larger units reveal more redundancy, but the DBMS must still support localized updates; the following intervals resolve this tension.

The board illustrates LZ77-style compression: repeated byte sequences are replaced with a back-reference and repeat count. Such schemes need a sufficiently large history window to find repetition; a tiny tuple may contain too little redundancy to compress well.

Compressing a large page or multi-page block improves ratio but makes a small update expensive: the system may need to decompress, modify, and recompress the whole unit, and the recompressed result may no longer fit its old space. Per-tuple compression weakens the compression ratio but preserves independent updates and stable page management.

The tuple is therefore a practical compression boundary. Slotted pages continue treating each tuple as an opaque byte range, so compression stays in the record-format layer rather than infecting lower-level page logic.

A slotted page needs only the byte length and location of a record. It does not interpret attributes, so compressed and uncompressed tuples use exactly the same page interface. This is a concrete payoff from layering.

Compression belongs above the slotted-page layer. The page machinery continues to handle insertion, relocation, and transactions for opaque records; the record layer alone decides how the attribute bytes are encoded.

General-purpose algorithms such as LZ77 plus Huffman coding are often too CPU-intensive for individual tuples and may find little repetition in such small inputs. If decompression dominates query time, compression has defeated its original performance purpose.

DBMS formats therefore favor simple, attribute-aware encodings that can be decoded with a few instructions. Byte-oriented codes are usually preferred over tightly packed variable-bit codes: they may consume slightly more space, but CPUs manipulate bytes much more cheaply.

The board uses adaptive Huffman coding as a cautionary example. Ordinary Huffman coding assigns short bit strings to frequent symbols but requires the decoder to know the tree. Adaptive coding updates an initially shared tree after every symbol, so compressor and decompressor reconstruct the same model without transmitting it.

The idea improves compression on short inputs, yet updating and traversing the tree for every symbol is complex and CPU-heavy. The professor’s implementation compressed successfully but made queries slower because decompression consumed the saved time—a reminder to evaluate full-system performance, not ratio alone.

Adaptive Huffman demonstrates why a theoretically elegant encoding can be wrong for a DBMS. Dynamic tree maintenance is complicated, and bit-level decoding requires many branches and shifts. The CPU overhead can exceed the bandwidth savings.

A practical system often accepts a weaker compression ratio and uses whole-byte codes. The exam-relevant criterion is net execution time: compression is beneficial only when fewer transferred and cached bytes compensate for encoding and decoding work.

Variable-length integer encoding stores a small length tag followed by only the necessary low-order bytes. Values that fit in one byte consume far less than a fixed four-byte integer, while large values fall back to the full representation.

One tag pattern can instead represent NULL with zero payload bytes, leaving other patterns for one-, two-, and four-byte integers. This loses the three-byte case but combines NULL representation and compression cheaply. The scheme works well when small magnitudes are common and remains fast because payload handling is byte-oriented.

Variable-length integers make formerly fixed attributes harder to locate because each field’s start depends on preceding compressed lengths. Group four two-bit length tags into one byte. Since that byte has only 256 possible values, a precomputed lookup table can return every field’s offset and size.

The table converts several branches and prefix sums into one indexed lookup plus simple address arithmetic. This is a recurring DBMS technique: spend a small fixed table to make a compact representation fast enough for every tuple access.

Dictionary compression factors repeated strings out of tuples. Each distinct value is stored once in a dictionary, and tuples store compact integer identifiers. Repeated city or street names then occupy one string plus many small IDs rather than many full copies.

The technique can dramatically reduce size because real datasets often repeat categorical text. Integer IDs are also cheaper to compare and may themselves use variable-length encoding. Dictionary maintenance and indirection add costs, but the encoding is especially attractive when the cardinality is far below the row count.

The board explains why dictionary compression remains useful even though normalization could remove repeated strings logically. Real applications often store redundant text, sometimes for portability or historical reasons, and may even encode numeric values as strings.

A DBMS cannot assume ideal schema design. Compression can recover some of the physical efficiency by factoring repeated values internally, but storing every type as text still pushes parsing and semantics into the application and should not be copied as a modern design.

A dictionary removes exact duplicate strings; prefix compression can go further by sharing common beginnings such as URL schemes or host names among different strings. Similar specialized encodings can exploit domain structure.

More aggressive compression is not automatically better. Each extra encoding layer increases CPU and access complexity, so choose the strongest scheme whose decompression remains cheaper than the bandwidth and cache misses it saves.

The lecture now moves from compact ordinary tuples to records that cannot fit on one fixed-size page. The remaining problem is how to represent documents, images, and other BLOB or CLOB values without abandoning page-based buffering and recovery.

This brief visual return bridges dictionary compression to long-record handling. Compression may shrink many values, but it cannot guarantee that every user-supplied record becomes smaller than a page.

A fixed page places a hard upper bound on an ordinary inline tuple. Some products reject larger rows, but users still need large binary or character values. SQL therefore provides BLOBs for opaque byte sequences and CLOBs for long text.

These types signal that the attribute requires out-of-line storage rather than an ordinary slot-sized record. The exact mechanism follows in the next recording; the important transition is that large-value support must coexist with fixed-size pages rather than replace them.
No aligned speech occurs in this brief closing board frame.

The recording resumes with a recap: slotted pages locate tuple byte ranges, while the record format splits fixed and variable data so each attribute is accessible efficiently. That ordinary layout is the baseline from which large, out-of-line values must deviate.

Compression can improve the ordinary record representation, but only by trading CPU work against reduced data movement. It does not solve the structural case where a value remains larger than one page.

Fixed-size pages simplify buffer management and recovery because every transfer and repair uses a known unit, but they cap inline tuple size below the page capacity. BLOB and CLOB types deliberately allow values far above that limit—for example, a user photo or long document.

A BLOB is treated as opaque bytes; a CLOB is long character data on which a system may offer limited text operations. DBMSs can support values from kilobytes to much larger sizes, but extremely large media may perform better in a file or object store. The implementation must preserve page-based internals while exposing a large logical value.

The naive representation splits one tuple across a linked chain of pages, continuing the large attribute wherever space remains. Although it can represent arbitrary size, it couples ordinary tuple access to an unbounded traversal.
This is the design to reject: a tuple ceases to be a small bufferable object, and every operator that handles it must understand partial records and page chains.

An unbounded page chain defeats predictable buffering. Reconstructing one logical tuple may require more frames than the buffer—or even more memory than the machine—while holding locks and coordinating recovery across all pages. A robust design must keep the main tuple bounded.

The board emphasizes that reading only part of a chained tuple is insufficient for normal tuple processing: the attribute is logically one value, so a naive operator may need every page resident simultaneously. This motivates separating the value from the tuple.

Store the ordinary tuple inline but replace the large attribute with a stable handle to a separate BLOB structure. Query operators can copy, join, or project that small handle without loading the large payload. The payload is retrieved only when the client actually requests its contents, sometimes through a dedicated streaming API.

This isolates complexity in the BLOB manager. Accessing the content costs an extra lookup and most SQL operations cannot inspect it cheaply, but buffering and intermediate results remain bounded regardless of BLOB size.

A flexible BLOB representation indexes payload pages in a B-tree-like structure by cumulative byte length. Leaves hold chunks; inner entries describe how many bytes lie in each subtree. Searching an offset descends logarithmically, and range access reads only the relevant leaves.

Store subtree lengths as relative values rather than absolute file offsets. Inserting or deleting bytes then changes only entries along the search path; later subtrees retain their local offsets. This supports efficient random reads and mid-value edits, but may be more functionality than ordinary SQL—which usually reads or replaces the whole BLOB—actually exposes.

A simpler BLOB header stores total length, an optional hash for fast inequality checks, and an extent list of `(start page, page count)` runs. The main tuple points to this header, and the extents identify all payload pages.

Growing extent sizes usually keeps the list short; only a pathological list needs chaining. This representation efficiently reads, deletes, or replaces the BLOB as one object but does not support convenient insertion or deletion in the middle. For a simple SQL interface, that limitation is often an acceptable price for much less metadata.

The next optimization recognizes that a type’s declared maximum says little about actual values. BLOB and CLOB columns can be enormous, yet many stored instances are short; the representation should avoid an out-of-line structure for those common cases.

Users often choose CLOB-like types because they do not want to guess a maximum `VARCHAR` length. A bound that is too small rejects legitimate data; very large bounds across many columns can violate a DBMS requirement that the maximum row fit on one page. Fixed `CHAR(n)` is not a good escape because it pads values and has surprising comparison behavior.

A text or oversized-attribute type offers a better contract: store ordinary short strings inline, but transparently move a rare long value out of line. PostgreSQL calls this TOAST. The key is to optimize actual length while retaining an effectively unbounded logical type.

Use a tiered BLOB representation. If the payload is shorter than the handle field, encode it directly inside that field. If it is larger but still fits on one page, point to a simple one-page BLOB record. Only values exceeding a page need an extent list or tree.

This preserves support for arbitrarily large values while making short values—which dominate many supposedly “large” columns—cheap. A variant stores text inline in the tuple until the row would overflow, then replaces the data with an out-of-line TID.
This title interval closes record storage and opens index structures. The next unit asks how to find selected tuples without scanning every page in the relation.

At this point the storage path is complete: slotted pages identify tuples, record layouts provide constant-time attributes, optional compression reduces movement, and tiered out-of-line storage handles long values. The lecture now adds structures that locate those tuples selectively.
Index structures are introduced as the alternative to reading a relation from beginning to end. Their useful access patterns—especially exact keys and ranges—are developed in the following chapter.

Without an index, a predicate such as `x = 7` requires a full table scan: visit every page, inspect every tuple, and test the condition. Runtime is linear in relation size even if only one row qualifies.
An access path stores additional organization that can jump to the relevant tuple identifiers. It pays space and update maintenance to make selective point or range queries much faster than scanning.
